newsitem.title: USA: Credit risk rising at large U.S. banks - OCC survey.
newsitem.headline: Credit risk rising at large U.S. banks - OCC survey.

text.p: Credit portfolios at large national banks in the United States are showing increased risk levels compared to a year ago, particularly in competitive areas such as the credit card business, according to a survey released on Wednesday.

"As compared with a year ago, at most of the banks surveyed the level of inherent credit risk has increased in one or more of the product components of their loan portfolios," the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, a bank regulatory agency, said in a summary of its second annual "Survey of Credit Underwriting Practices."
The survey, conducted by bank examiners, looked at the country's 82 largest national banks.
The trend of higher-risk portfolios was present in lending to both consumers and to commercial establishments, the OCC said, but it was more apparent in some areas than in others.

"Increased levels of credit risk were most frequently noted in the credit card and indirect components of banks' retail portfolio and in the middle market and syndicated/national credit components of commercial portfolios," the agency said.
The rise in credit risk is a "warning signal" that examiners are monitoring, said Scott Calhoun, deputy comptroller for risk evaluation at the OCC.

"We are keeping our antenna up," he said. However, asked about the odds that the credit situation could spur a large-scale crisis should the currently healthy economy suffer a setback, Calhoun said that was unlikely.
"I don't view this as the next meltdown," he said.
Looking at overall lending standards, the survey showed that in most cases they were unchanged compared to a year ago.
Still, in the area of commercial lending, most of the banks that did change their practices loosened standards.

In commercial lending, 19 percent of the banks altered their standards in the commercial sector, including 14 percent of the institutions that had easier standards and five percent which had stricter conditions.
Twenty-six percent of the banks changed standards in the retail area. Of those, half loosened standards while the other half tightend them.

In the area of credit-card lending, the OCC said many of the very largest banks began tightening their standards in early 1996, although a number of banks below the top tier continued to relaxed them.

Looking at the link between lending standards and the quality of credit, Jeri Gilland, a bank examiner who is chairwoman of an OCC panel on credit matters, said there is a relationship but she noted it takes time for changes in credit standards to affect the quality of a bank's portfolio.

"What we see in the credit-card area is reflecting what happened in the third and fourth quarters of 1995," Gilland said. Concerning the trends in current lending standards, she added, "It will be 12 to 18 months before you see the results of this."
